item.title: 'Special K' Didn’t Retire When Spravato Arrived
item.description:
Ketamine

'Special K' Didn’t Retire When Spravato Arrived

A spotlight on ketamine, incapacitation, and the need for safeguards.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Ketamine may treat depression. Misuse can cause incapacitation, addiction, and vulnerability to exploitation.
  • An addiction history calls for careful assessment and consent before ketamine and monitoring during and after.
  • Spravato administration is supervised and monitored. "Off-label" ketamine also needs these FDA safeguards.
  • A prescription doesn’t erase ketamine’s risks. Celebrity use is not evidence of safety.

A former Cornell student identified as Jane Doe alleges she was drinking, given ketamine, and sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in October 2024. She said that when she returned to her sorority house, she answered her sisters’ questions about what happened with one word: “Ketamine.” The allegations remain contested, and investigations are underway. The case reminds us, or should, of ketamine’s lurid past. Known as Special K, the drug was nefariously used by some to incapacitate people, mostly females, to exploit them sexually.

I have discussed ketamine’s dark side here before.

Ketamine's History
Source: Mark Gold, MD with permission

Ketamine became an invaluable battlefield medicine during the Vietnam War, in surgery, emergency and pain medicine, and trauma care. By the late 1980s, ketamine had entered its rave-nightclub period. Federal Schedule III control of the drug followed in 1999. Then came Yale’s pioneering antidepressant study.

Ketamine produces dissociation—feeling separated from the body and surroundings. In medicine, this helps patients tolerate painful surgeries. Elsewhere, impaired movement and memory can leave someone unable to protect themselves. At high recreational doses, users describe the “K-hole”—profound disconnection and difficulty moving, speaking, or responding.

For drug abusers, disconnection is the main attraction of ketamine. And for an opportunistic predator, ketamine means an opening to exploitation.

Ketamine blocks NMDA glutamate receptors and stimulates the opioid system.

NYU researcher Joseph Palamar surveyed New York City nightclub attendees, and ketamine use rose from 7.4 percent in 2017 to 14.3 percent in 2024. Nearly double. Young people, clubgoers, and festivalgoers use ketamine. Its psychiatric reputation may make that escape sound safer than it is.

Sexual Vulnerability and Ketamine

The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) lists ketamine among substances encountered in drug-facilitated sexual assault. Alcohol is much more commonly implicated. Combining ketamine with alcohol increases the risks of severe impairment, unconsciousness, and potentially dangerous breathing problems.

GHB and benzodiazepines, including flunitrazepam—Rohypnol, or “roofies”—are also listed.

Ketamine can be a colorless, odorless liquid, although street ketamine is also sold as a powder.

Not every assault begins with a spiked drink. UNODC also recognizes exploitation after voluntary substance use. Consent to ketamine is not consent to sex. If drugging or assault is suspected, seek medical care promptly. Toxicology testing is time-sensitive.

From Bangkok to Today

While visiting Thailand as a University of Florida professor, I met with local DEA personnel concerned about ketamine misuse and trafficking. Their experiences with ketamine were warnings. Ketamine was cheap, widely used as a club drug, and capable of leaving people incapacitated and vulnerable to rape and sexual exploitation. Lost weekends. Sometimes far worse.

The U.N. reports ketamine mixtures sold in Thailand as “happy water” and “K-powdered milk.” Marketing names. Like “pink cocaine,” which actually contains ketamine; these illicit concoctions, drug mixtures, and doses vary. Buyer beware.

Ketamine Abuse and Diversion

In 2016, my USC colleagues and I reviewed ketamine abuse and diversion, three years before Spravato’s approval for depression. We described cognitive, addiction, and psychiatric problems, sexual assault concerns, severe urinary tract injuries, and gastrointestinal and liver complications from ketamine use.

“Doctors use it” is hardly a recommendation for college students considering ketamine abuse. Doctors also use scalpels. Context again. A party has no emergency recovery room. Friends may also be intoxicated, unable to recognize trouble or help.

Ketamine addiction is also very real. Craving, escalating use, unsuccessful attempts to stop, and continued use regardless of harms are symptoms meriting an addiction evaluation. Opioid-like withdrawal symptoms aren’t required.

Actor Matthew Perry’s Death From Ketamine

Perry’s death in 2023 made ketamine’s risks painfully clear. The medical examiner identified the acute effects of ketamine as the cause.

Ketamine's sedation, dissociation, or unconsciousness can become deadly in a bathtub, hot tub, or pool. An incapacitated person may be unable to keep their head above water or escape.

People entrusted to care for Matthew Perry exploited his addiction for profit. His vulnerability became their business opportunity. What happened to the Hippocratic Oath?

Perry’s toxicology showed buprenorphine, a medication used to treat opioid use disorder (OUD). An SUD history is a major warning flag when considering ketamine for depression. It demands looking for alternatives, careful assessment, supervised treatment, and close follow-up for misuse. Celebrity status should never lower those standards. Celebrities are vulnerable humans, too.

Reports that Presley Gerber received prescribed ketamine before his death at 27 raise the same question: Who protects the patient? His cause of death remains undetermined.

Celebrity use can become an inadvertent endorsement. Familiar face. Unfamiliar risks. Readers may remember who used ketamine and forget what happened next. A famous user is not evidence of safety or effectiveness.

Ketamine and Depression

Spravato is the FDA-approved esketamine nasal spray used for treatment-resistant depression and certain other depressive symptoms. It requires a certified medical setting, supervision, at least two hours of monitoring, and assessment before discharge. It should never be regarded like ordering take-out from local fast foods. Ketamine treatment is approved for anesthesia, but for depression remains off-label. Patients may feel “high” with either IV ketamine or Spravato administered at standard antidepressant doses. Some patients experience euphoria. Others find the experience unpleasant or terrifying. Dissociation is not inherently pleasurable.

Off-label prescribing isn’t illegal. But a prescription does not erase addiction, exploitation, or toxicity risks. Patient pre-screening, ketamine dose, setting, and supervision during and after treatment all matter.

Recovery Requires Much More

Patients with early-onset or longstanding addictions need sustained care. A miracle drug to reverse the addiction clock? Still waiting. Today, evidence-based treatment, follow-up, and recovery support are available.

Physician health programs combine intensive evaluation and addiction treatment with years of monitoring, random drug testing, recovery support, and accountability, a model showing what is possible.

Ask!

On October 13, 2026, Cornell announced it would suspend frat parties and social events for the rest of the academic year. They also announced a review of fraternity life and the culture surrounding sexual violence. It also pledged expanded support for survivors.

Universities should be asking about drug-facilitated rape, alcohol and ketamine use on campus—consider wastewater testing to help track it. If they do not do a complete assessment, they will miss an important opportunity for change.

Campus outreach should name ketamine and its possible use to facilitate sexual assault. Administrators and campus police need training and support to spot and react to suspected drug-facilitated assaults. Students need prompt medical care and an empathetic, clear, accessible way to report. Closing the fraternity party calendar is a step. Changing the culture takes more.

item.title: The Link Between Relationships and Meaning in Life
item.description:
Aging

The Link Between Relationships and Meaning in Life

Social connections become more significant and important as we age.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Experiencing life as having meaning in older years contributes to health and holistic well-being.
  • Quality relationships are strongly associated with meaning in life for older people.
  • Especially with older adults, individual autonomy and meaningful activity are important to well-being,
  • Technology is helpful, but no substitute for in-person contact.

Over the years, relational communication has evolved from primarily in-person to hybrid telephone-computer engagement, to real-time texting. Decades ago, virtual interaction was viewed as a young person’s game. Not anymore. Older people routinely use technology for many of the same reasons as their younger counterparts: to connect and communicate, to work and to play, and to explore the world and keep up with neighborhood news. As we age and begin to face physical challenges, however, technology can provide unique assistance in compensating for decreased capacities, allowing people to maintain meaning, autonomy, and quality of life. Research explains.

Source: Image by Alsu from Pixabay

Making Meaning Through Relationships and Autonomy

Suvi-Maria Saarelainen et al. (2022) studied the importance of relationships later in life.[i] They began by acknowledging that experiencing life as having meaning in our older years contributes to health and holistic well-being. Noting that many people live in their own homes while experiencing reduced capacities over time, they recognize the need to discover new ways to prompt well-being in old age. Studying online data collected from discussion groups on a channel called Service TV (STV), they found that relationality is strongly associated with meaning in life for older people.

One area of increasing relevance as we age that contributes to maintaining meaning is personal independence. Recognizing that individual autonomy and meaningful activity are important to well-being, Saarelainen et al. explain that respect and support for the autonomy of aging individuals is critical. Because many older people desire to remain in their own homes even while experiencing diminished capacity, family support is key, as loved ones can assist in choosing and negotiating workable, autonomous living arrangements to facilitate aging parents and relatives maintaining quality of life.

Saarelainen et al. also recognize that relationships impact individual sense of meaning. They report that older people felt a relational gap more strongly when they were distanced from family, lacked same age peers, or were bereaved or widowed. On the other hand, participating in activities with peers produced deep joy and a sense of connectedness. For participants, STV provided a way to create meaningful relationships, demonstrating that relationality can be created and maintained through technology.

Saarelainen et al. conclude that many people experience meaning in life through a network of relationships. Meaningfulness is reinforced through having opportunities to connect and share, feel a sense of belonging, and be cared for. Loss of meaning is created through vulnerability, feeling different, and grieving the loss of loved ones who have passed away.

Technology Cannot Replace Loved Ones

Relationally, we don’t grow out of craving human connection—in person. Saarelainen et al. note that although technology facilitates sharing and caring for older people, there are ethical issues to consider. Technologically facilitated care deprives patients of relational satisfaction only possible in person. Indeed, their study participants reminded them that phone calls do not replace live meetings with family members, a reality that translates into the use of technical-assisted care. Healthy connections can bring meaningfulness, belonging, and joy later in life, although it will not replace meeting people in person.

So, with aging loved ones with decreasing capabilities, we can help maintain meaningfulness through autonomy by providing technological assistance and reliable virtual connection through easy-to-use communication. And then enjoy timeless love and laughter through visiting in person as often as we can.

item.title: Trust Is More Than Honesty: 4 Ways to Build It
item.description:
Trust

Trust Is More Than Honesty: 4 Ways to Build It

It’s the little things that tell your partner, “I can count on you.”

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Trust grows when your partner knows their feelings and well-being matter to you.
  • Honesty and follow-through help your partner to feel safe counting on you.
  • Small, everyday gestures of care can matter more than grand romantic displays.
  • Repair builds trust through empathy, accountability, and meaningful changes in behavior.

What is trust, really?

As a couples therapist, I'd define it as the feeling that your well-being matters to another person, and that this care shows up in their actions.

We can fully trust someone else only when we know, deep down in our core, that how we feel matters to them — that what we need and want matters and will be prioritized by another.

Breaches of trust, such as infidelity, are so damaging because they shake the foundation we stand on. To feel safe, we need to feel that our partner considers us in their actions and takes the impact of their choices on us seriously. When we get the message that our feelings haven't been prioritized, it can shatter the relationship to the point where partners question whether they can assume their partner is ever looking out for them at all.

To build or rebuild a strong foundation of trust in your relationship, make sure to do these four things

1. Be honest, always. When we lie, our partner has no way to know if future words are fibs or truth. This will make things much harder for both of you. Trust is, above all, the safety of being able to assume positive intent in our relationship. Even small lies can create massive ruptures in trust, because they introduce uncertainty about the future. If you have struggled with honesty in your relationship, it's never too late to turn things around by starting now.

2. Make sure your words and actions align. If you say you'll do something, no matter how big or small, follow through. This shows your partner, "I'm there for you. You can count on me." Align your words and actions so your partner doesn't have to wonder whether you'll be there for them. Reliability brings predictability to the relationship, which is one of the most important ingredients for building safety. Just like being afraid of the dark, as humans, we fear the unknown. Be known to your partner.

3. Even in the little moments, show your partner that their feelings matter. For example, if your partner tells you they had a long day, why not stop by the store on the way home and bring them home their favorite treat? Little things like this show that you care about your partner's well-being. In my work with couples, I've learned that small gestures of care are even more impactful than flashy or expensive ones.

4. Work on repair. Mistakes are inevitable, as we are all flawed humans. Responding to your partner's hurt with kindness, empathy, and full attention strengthens trust, while responding with defensiveness weakens it. Ruptures are inevitable and offer opportunities to deepen trust. Acknowledge the impact of your actions, listen before defending your intentions, and make a plan for behavior change. For example, if you forget an important commitment and your partner is frustrated, listen as they share their hurt so they feel heard. And then, share how you'll keep better track of commitments next time.

Trust builds when we know our needs and feelings matter to our partner and will be heard and responded to. Show your partner that their feelings and needs matter to you with small gestures of care, authenticity, and keeping your word. Your partner will feel safe enough to assume the positive intent behind your actions, and you'll both benefit from a more secure, peaceful, and joyful bond.

item.title: Dictation Apps Are Not "AI." They're Accessibility Tools.
item.description:
Neurodiversity

Dictation Apps Are Not "AI." They're Accessibility Tools.

Once again, in debates about tech, disabled students are left out in the cold.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Debates about any technology use must account for disability, including neurodiversity.
  • Neurodivergent (and other disabled) students rely on assistive technology like dictation.
  • Dictation apps are not LLMs. They’ve been around for decades, and neurodivergent people need them.
Source: Unknown Creator / Pixabay

A few weeks ago, I shattered my sacrum, the lowest part of your spine, located in the center of your pelvis. Yes, I was doing a physical activity when the injury occurred, but I also have a chronic disability that makes me more prone to this type of injury. It is a massive, messy break.

I’m not sure if you’ve ever had to lie flat on your back for a long period of time, but even with all occupational therapy tools, it is difficult to write. Which is a problem when you are a full-time writer and a creative writing professor. I have two books forthcoming next year with copyedits due, and I have two book proposals that editors have requested. I have articles. More.

My work is so hard because I can’t sit at my desk. Typing is very difficult. But as of last week, I made a big discovery, and I am grateful.

I found a new, highly accurate dictation software that has made my disabled life more accessible. It is called Wispr Flow (or just Wispr). I’ve wanted to tell everyone all about it.

But then I learned that not everyone likes Wispr. On August 19, 2026, The New York Times published a hit piece about Wispr by Amy X. Wang. I was shocked to see the negative headline: “Everyone’s Using This A.I. Dictation App That I Want to Murder With a Hammer.”

There are many problems with Wang’s piece and its argument, but it is also very, very ableist.

As I’ve written before, these myriad debates over the ethics of technology throw disabled students (and others) under the bus. The Times piece does the same. Is Wispr, a seemingly innocuous dictation software, so special that it deserves an entire article in the paper of record? Is it killing good writing, as Wang asserts? Does it deserve the amount of vitriol it receives in the column? The answers are straightforward: No, No, and No.

Dictation isn't new

Wispr, as dictation software goes, breaks little new ground. Wang notes this herself: “I hate that so many people in the world are lauding this like it’s the greatest invention.” She’s right. It’s not a new “invention.” It’s just the latest iteration of a tool that’s been around for decades—or millennia, depending on how you look at it.

Modern computer dictation software is decades old. Dragon NaturallySpeaking, the first big player in this area, was released 30 years ago. Before Dragon—before software—we had typists in the steno pool, transcribing dictation from the little tapes dropped on their desks by Mad Men.

Wang calls Wispr an “A.I. Dictation App,” while admitting, "I’m actually not sure how A.I. is involved in this.” The answer: It isn’t, at least not in the way most people think about AI. Wispr doesn’t write your words for you; it transcribes, just as other dictation apps have transcribed over the years.

I have been dictating my writing for decades, for a variety of reasons, most related to my neurodiversity or other disability issues. Until I discovered Wispr, I used the built-in dictation feature on my iPhone, or the accessibility feature on macOS, but those tools are dodgy at best. Finding dictation software that is effective has been a godsend. Wang agrees, writing that, unlike the dictation feature on her own iPhone, which she calls “abysmal,” Wispr Flow’s "speed and accuracy are pretty astonishing. You can quite literally whisper to it at the softest possible volume, like I’m doing right now, and the transcript will be almost perfect.”

So what’s the problem? It appears from this description that Wispr is a solid dictation app that’s a step up from the one many of us already use. It is higher quality and does a better job. Sure, it’s overhyped by its marketing team, but who cares?

Yes, dictation is writing

Wang believes that the act of dictation itself makes writing worse, and that this worse-writing problem is an epidemic related to dictation. Regarding Wispr, she writes, “I think it’s making everyone sound a little like an idiot, and now everybody has to read everyone else’s idiot words.”

As a person (me) who must use dictation because of neurodiversity and physical disability, those words were a gut punch.

When I write books, essays, poetry, or whatever genre I’m tackling on a particular day, I use every tool at my disposal in the creative process. I handwrite, type, and dictate. Sometimes, I dictate while walking, sometimes while sitting at my desk—the point is, I do whatever it takes to get the words out of my head and into my dirty first draft.

If we want to get scientific about it, each type of writing uses different neural pathways of the brain to access creativity. I am lucky that, usually, I get to use all three.

Wang argues that revision is integral to writing, and that is true. No one should use a dictated first draft as a final draft, just as no one should use any first draft as a final draft, no matter what medium they used to create it. However, Wang wrote her column using dictation, but did not edit. She explains, “I’m looking at the paragraphs above, and I’m really itching to edit them. A lot of these sentences are bad. But the whole point of Wispr Flow is that you don’t edit.”

In all my decades of dictation, no matter what software I used, I never avoided editing. That’s just silly. So it's no surprise, given that she did not edit the column, that the writing is not very good. As she admits, “I’m reading these paragraphs above again now and I think I sound like an idiot?” [sic]

To answer her semi-question, she does indeed at least sound like a poor writer. But she already knows why and has told us why: It's because she didn’t revise her dictated writing. But why not? Her answer would have earned her poor feedback from me back when I was teaching first-year argumentation. Wang composed an admittedly poorly written column using Wispr software, and then blamed the software instead of her process.

But it is not Wispr’s fault if the column is poor; it's the fault of the choices the writer made. She could have dictated her column, revised it as usual, and it would have likely been better. Had she typed her column, she would never have turned it in without revision. She’s a professional writer.

The column's weak argument, though, is overshadowed by my biggest problem with it: It is ableist.

Dictation software has always been an accessibility tool

Like all dictation software that has come before it, Wispr is an incredible accessibility tool. That it was invented by tech bros should not drive people away from it. Many accessibility tools were invented by tech bros. The laptop I’m using right now is one of them.

But it's not only physically disabled people who benefit from dictation software. For writers with dyslexia and other language acquisition disabilities, many of whom I teach, dictation is an essential accessibility tool.

“I wish I could describe elegantly how much I hate [Wispr] with some kind of handy, clever metaphor," Wang writes, "but that kind of creativity comes to me through writing with my hands.” But tell me: How many people cannot write with their hands because of an impairment that prevents it? Many of my autistic and ADHD students struggle with dysgraphia, for example, which affects their ability to hand-write.

Or shall we conjure Stephen Hawking and ask him about how his writing and creativity are linked only to his hands? What about Jean-Dominique Bauby of The Diving Bell and the Butterfly?

Wang prefers her hands, but that preference is a privilege. She writes, “Writing is a rigorous process to understand your own thoughts and then lay those thoughts out in a way that convinces or inspires or moves other people. But speaking is not that process.” Of course it is: People have been talking creatively and in ways that move people since the dawn of humanity, long before we learned to scratch out symbols on rocks. We are storytelling animals. And we are, historically, oral storytellers. These oral traits are part of what it means to be human, and they have nothing to do with writing with pen on paper.

But setting anthropology aside, dictation’s job, like any process one uses to create a dirty first draft, is not to “lay out your thoughts” in a “rigorous” way. It is to get them on the page so that you can revise them into something that does those things.

That’s a gift that dictation software gives to neurodivergent and other disabled people. I always teach my students that dictation is an option when they get stuck, or if they've never felt good at writing. They come back to me the next day eyes bright, as though I've opened the door to a new world. "I wrote a thousand words," one said. "It felt like magic."

With powerful dictation software, many more people have access to words who might not have otherwise. A person who struggles to write on a keyboard or with a pen because of an impairment finds themselves able to write. For that writer, dictation software is nothing short of a miracle.

item.title: Finding Purpose in the Age of AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Finding Purpose in the Age of AI

Leaning into what feels human.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • AI has threatened our purpose in life.
  • Consider what makes us human and use that to find purpose.
  • Being in touch with death helps us live.

I’d stopped writing Psychology Today posts, at least for a period of time. Part of what I love about writing is the pleasure in the discovery, in making unique connections, in framing an idea in a new way, in stitching ideas together, and feeling like I had something original to offer. With AI, that sense of discovery and mastery has felt diminished. Couldn't people just explore these ideas on their own? Were my ideas original enough? I wanted to add something new to the conversation, but worried that there was a far superior conversationalist.

It has me wondering (along with the rest of humanity): As AI becomes more capable, what will give our lives meaning and purpose?

Source: wal_172619 / Pixabay

Will AI take our jobs? Can it do our work better than us? Why are we still bothering when there is a tool that is superior and fully accessible, with no energy on our part? Could AI even be a better therapist or friend? I like to think not, but the threat is not entirely unfounded.

It also raises the question, what is it that makes us human and how are we distinct? In a recent podcast from The Daily, “When AI Comes for Your Purpose in Life,” professor of mathematics at Cornell University Steven Strogatz grapples with this question, as AI has been solving the world’s most vexing math problems. You ride his emotions throughout until the end when he explores what it is to be human. He highlights the ephemeral nature of our lives. We are born and we die. And we get to decide what we do in the middle.

We can use our five senses to explore our world and be present to our lives. We can turn to people — and not technology — to feel human and focus on building loving relationships. We can keep in mind that life will end. And, while it may sound doomsday, that is not the intention. It is the opposite: When we are in touch with our mortality, we can fully appreciate and have gratitude for our lives. It can be grounding, and can give us much-needed perspective when we find ourselves in the weeds of life. We want to find a balance — neither being consumed by ruminative thoughts of death, nor ignoring it, but rather acknowledging it so that we can create meaning in the middle. We get to decide where we want to put our energy in the limited time we are allotted.

So here is my human touch Psychology Today post To be human, let’s:

  1. Turn toward each other.
  2. Focus our attention on our five senses as we explore our world.
  3. Acknowledge the end, so we can appreciate the in-between and maintain a balanced perspective.
  4. Explore how we feel, what’s important, and move towards our unique constellation of values, so that in the end we can say, “It was a life well lived.”

item.title: Got Integrity?
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Got Integrity?

Integrity is striking a harmonious balance within ourselves and our environment.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Integrity is a concept that can be insightfully applied to buildings and people.
  • In both cases, integrity is a consequence of how designs and materials stay within acceptable tolerances.
  • Integrity in a person is a matter of virtuous moral character.
  • Being inconsistent on significant matters can threaten a person’s integrity.

“Integrity” is one of those terms that has multiple meanings and applications. The concept comes from the Latin word, integritatem, which means soundness, wholeness, or completeness. These traits can be found in both buildings and people.

The integrity of buildings

The integrity of a building depends on many factors. A building’s design with its load-bearing walls, materials, joists, and foundations, and the materials used in them, all play a part. Different materials such as concrete, steel, wood, and glass have different tolerances. In architecture and building, tolerance is the allowable deviation from specified plans, dimensions, alignment, and load; glass, for example, can withstand only so much pressure before it cracks, steel will start to buckle under too heavy a weight, and concrete can withstand only so much water.

The tolerances of the different materials as they relate to each other through the design and the environment determine the safety and security of the building. Staying within the allowable tolerances for these materials makes a building sound, which is integrity.

The integrity of a building neither implies nor relies upon unity. Nor does it imply that integrity is pure, unmixed, or unadulterated. Seamlessness has little to do with integrity. No one element determines it; a solid foundation doesn’t make a house sound if the joists in the attic are rotting and the roof is going to collapse.

Integrity is dynamic and relational. Some designs intentionally include features to compensate for changes in the tolerance of any one element or the overall tolerance of the building.

The integrity of people

The integrity of a person is similarly a matter of design, action, mixed elements, and tolerances.

We humans are a mixture of many different elements. We are embodied creatures with needs, desires, and appetites. We also have cognitive capacities, imaginations, commitments, values, and relations to others. Each of these has a tolerance, and a person of integrity recognizes them. Each of us represents a constantly shifting balance of these elements. All thoughts can be driven from a person’s mind when they experience a leg cramp. A calm demeanor may enable someone to appreciate something in others that they may otherwise miss.

Integrity attaches not only to particular actions but to the character of the person acting. One becomes a person of integrity by acting in ways that embody integrity. As Aristotle (384-322 BCE) notes, we become who we are by what we do habitually. The “who we are" is our moral character. Our moral character becomes firm and stable but not rigid; it directs our actions. As Aristotle notes, virtuous acts can only be done by people of virtuous character.

Since we humans are a mixture of different elements, our virtues will be as well. Some virtues such as temperance or moderation relate to our bodies and their needs and appetites. Other virtues such as compassion attach to our relations to others. The virtue of perspicacity attaches to our reason; it is the ability to have keen insights into complex or difficult situations.

One does not become a person of integrity accidentally; one needs a design paired with deliberate action that is responsive to environment. We have to construct our character. As Montaigne (1533-1592) notes, "To compose our character is our duty, not to compose books, and to win, not battles and provinces, but order and tranquility in our conduct. Our great and glorious masterpiece is to live appropriately."

Integrity allows us to live appropriately, which means that we are able to adjust to changes in our own selves and changes in our lives. The design of our lives needs to consider that much is beyond our control. We need to endure what we cannot avoid and accept that times in our lives will be sweet, bitter, and bittersweet.

A person of integrity lives within the tolerances of her different elements. Many times, those elements will be harmonious. At other times they will be benignly inconsistent. We are all full of inconsistencies, but that doesn’t affect our integrity. We can have integrity but not be seamless and totally smooth.

When inconsistencies become too significant, they can begin to exceed our tolerances. These inconsistencies can cause cracks and fissures that, over time, challenge a person’s integrity. To avoid this, a person needs to know herself in a profound way.

Self-knowledge is crucial to becoming and remaining a person of integrity. A person who knows her inconsistencies or weaknesses can, like the architect, build in some additional protective features to remain within her tolerances.

Integrity in people and in buildings is an ongoing achievement that requires regular inspection and maintenance. Conditions around both humans and buildings change regularly, which means integrity ought not to be taken for granted. Doing so risks exceeding tolerance.

item.title: The 3 Pillars of Happiness According to Science
item.description:
Happiness

The 3 Pillars of Happiness According to Science

Good relationships, meaning, and work can help you build a happier life.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Having good relationships is the most important pillar of happiness.
  • Knowing the meaning of your life and acting accordingly enhances happiness.
  • Enhance your happiness through your work by earning your success and benefitting others.
  • No one is always happy, but we can do things that improve our level of happiness.

What does it take to increase our happiness? There are three pillars of happiness: (1) good relationships, (2) meaning, and (3) work (if you're a student, that is your "work").

Good Relationships

Good relationships are overwhelmingly the most important pillar of happiness. The longest research study of happiness, healthfulness, and well-being is The Harvard Study of Adult Development. It showed that "Among the many predictors of health and happiness, from good diet to exercise to level of income, a life of good relationships stands out for its power and consistency (Waldinger, 2023).

Good relationships are critical for enhancing happiness, including in old age, even if we are dying and in pain. Palliative care physicians reviewed their patients' experiences and concluded, "social connection was the most important element of happiness at the end of life" (Beng, 2022).

We should treat our relationships with family, friends, co-workers, and others with care. It helps to write down the names of everyone we consider part of our meaningful relationships. Then, ask yourself if you are proactive in nurturing your relationships. Make it your responsibility.

Money and Happiness

What role does money play in happiness? Having enough money to meet our fundamental survival needs (food, shelter, clothing, and the like) adds to our happiness. However, once you reach the middle class in your society, more money does not make you happier.

However, there are three things that money can buy that increase happiness. One is using money to benefit others. The second is to buy experiences rather than things (e.g., take your kids on vacation rather than buying a newer car). The third is to buy time, i.e., pay someone else to do something that needs to be done that you don't like to do.

For example, you hate mowing your large lawn. If you can afford to pay someone else to mow it, you can use the time you saved to do something else.

A Meaningful Life

Meaning is the second pillar of happiness. It is important for both happiness and health. "Individuals who perceive their lives as full of meaning live longer, healthier, and happier lives than those less inclined to view their lives as meaningful" (Routledge, 2021).

According to Harvard's Arthur Brooks, meaning consists of three elements: coherence, purpose, and significance (Brooks, 2026). Many people find it helpful to use a structured approach to discover the meaning of their lives. They reflect on the three elements of meaning, write down their thoughts, and think about their current and future lives (Schippers, 2019).

Here are good questions to ask yourself about each of the three elements:

Coherence refers to how the parts of your life fit together. Ask yourself: How do all the different aspects of my life fit together and define me?

Purpose refers to what you are here to do and what you are intended to be. What are your goals? What is the point of your existence?

Significance refers to why and how you matter to yourself and others. Do I make a difference in the world? If I went away, would anyone care?

There are additional ways to find the meaning of your life. Religious belief often has meaning built into it. Some people find a philosophy, such as Stoicism or Buddhism, to be helpful. Mindfulness and meditation can also help.

Work (If You're a Student, School Is Your "Work.")

There are two important aspects of work that increase happiness: (1) earning your success and (2) making your work beneficial to others.

An example from school demonstrates what is meant by earning your success. Imagine two students taking a course together. One student has studied hard for her final exam and gets an A. The second student does not study for the exam but cheats and gets an A. Only one earned her success.

Thinking about your work, ask yourself, "How can my work help others?" Some work, like nursing, has an obvious way to do that. What about bricklaying?

Imagine a bricklayer planning to do such a great job laying bricks that the structure will be attractive and safe. He can understand how that benefits others.

Final Thoughts

We cannot be happy all the time. However, we can be happier if we give attention to the three pillars of happiness. Of the three, good relationships are clearly the most important.

item.title: Pornography Is Not a Public Health Crisis
item.description:
Pornography

Pornography Is Not a Public Health Crisis

The real issue is the lack of comprehensive sex education.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • The narratives on porn provoke fear and shame, but porn does not meet the criteria for a public health crisis.
  • The narratives on porn confuse causation and correlation. The body of research finds weak causal evidence.
  • Porn does not cause sexual dysfunction, addiction, or aggression.
  • The real public health crisis may be the lack of comprehensive sex education and porn literacy.
Source: ibreakstock/ iStock

Since Utah (a state with high religiosity) declared pornography a "public health crisis" in 2016, more than a dozen US states have passed similar resolutions, and the phrase now surfaces in UK debates. The language provokes much fear, and combined with poor sex education, the narrative becomes powerful because when people are afraid, they can become vulnerable to believing misinformation. The language borrows the authority of epidemiology and implies a measurable, population-wide harm on the scale of tobacco, opioids, or obesity. However, the claim does not stand up to the actual standards held by public health itself.

What makes something a public health crisis

Public health crises are defined by evidence: rising mortality or morbidity, plausible causation, and a burden of harm that can be counted across a population. Opioid deaths, the HIV epidemic, and smoking-related cancers meet that bar.

The state resolutions on pornography were not built on new epidemiological data. They were symbolic and non-binding, and largely drafted with advocacy groups (many of which had religious moral imperatives). Nelson and Rothman (2020) argue that porn does not meet the criteria for a public health crisis. Other reports on this topic came to the same conclusion. Pointing the finger at porn risks diverting attention from the real issue: improving comprehensive sex education, including porn literacy.

Indeed, it could be argued that a major lack of sex education is the actual ongoing public health crisis that governments seem to be reluctant to address properly. But it is also documented that some anti-porn campaigns can cause real harm too, making men feel shame for their viewing of pornography, and it is shame, not porn, that can deteriorate people’s mental health to the point of suicidality. While the narrative of “porn is a public health crisis” sound like a virtuous endeavor on the surface, it might actually do more harm than good, and it is not evidence-based.

The causal evidence is weak

Much of the research cited for the public health crisis confuses causation and correlation. There are indeed correlations but no causation. People who watch more pornography have diverse levels of sexual desire, sexual functioning, relationship satisfaction, and those differences are not caused by watching pornography because they can be associated with multiple other factors (correlations).

Research on sexual aggression is mixed, with some studies reporting a small association between pornography and aggressive attitudes, while others show the opposite: People who watch more porn have more egalitarian attitudes towards women. There are even some studies suggesting that there are fewer sexual crimes in countries where porn is more widely available. These are also not claiming causation: It does not mean that pornography reduces the risk of sexual aggression, but it does mean that it is pretty impossible to consider pornography as an epidemic and public health crisis.

"Porn addiction" is not an endorsed diagnosis

The crisis narrative leans heavily on the idea of “pornography addiction.” Yet the DSM-5 does not recognise “porn addiction” as a disorder, due to lack of scientific evidence. The ICD-11 recognises “compulsive sexual behaviour disorder” (CSBD), classifying it as an impulse-control disorder, not an addiction.

ICD-11 also states that distress arising solely from moral disapproval of one's sexual behaviour is not sufficient for diagnosis. That caveat matters. Research repeatedly finds that believing in being “addicted to porn” is predicted more strongly by religiosity and moral incongruence than by how much pornography a person actually watches.

For many people, the distress comes from a conflict between their values and their behaviour. For others, pornography viewing may become compulsive, as it is a coping strategy for emotional regulation. Clinicians can help with that, but it is not evidence of a population-wide pathology.

Erectile dysfunction claims don't hold up

Popular accounts link pornography to a wave of erectile problems in young men. Large studies have not found a consistent relationship between pornography viewing and erectile function, and the popular term PIED (porn-induced erectile dysfunction) has been disproved multiple times. However, the shame induced by sex-negative narratives/society may be a central factor for sexual dysfunction, as well as relationship factors, poor mental health, and medical factors.

The costs of the crisis framing

Calling pornography a public health crisis is not harmless rhetoric. It can induce or amplify shame, which tends to entrench compulsive patterns rather than resolve them. It can lead people to self-diagnose an addiction they do not have and push them towards "recovery" programmes that are not evidence-based, some with hidden religiosity and some that have been documented as iatrogenic.

It also distracts from issues where the evidence is stronger and action is achievable: better inclusive life-long sex education, including porn literacy.

A more useful frame

The narrative and research on pornography are biased because they tend to prioritise the negative aspects of pornography, and they approach the subject as though porn is a monolith. There are multiple types of porn, from problematic misogynistic porn, harmful porn depicting non-consensual acts, to ethical porn which can enhance people’s well-being.

The truth is that not all porn is bad, and sometimes there can even be benefits to watching some types of porn. For example, a study finds that queer people watching queer porn can be a source of meaningful well-being. Another study finds that young people felt pornographies offered a more diverse representation of body types than other media. A study suggests that women who watch pornography solo experience more positive emotions and fewer negative emotions, and partnered watching was associated with lower levels of negative emotions and higher levels of positive emotions.

However, pornography does not come without risks. A lot of media can have risks, in fact, not just porn. Some individuals do struggle with compulsive viewing due to underlying emotional disturbance and shame, and, of course, children should not be exposed to explicit sexual materials.

These real concerns are best met with targeted clinical support and porn literacy education: the same evidence-based methods used for other sexual health issues. Treating pornography as a sexual health topic rather than a public health crisis allows nuance, reduces stigma and keeps the focus on what actually helps.

item.title: The Intellectual Dust Bowl
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Intellectual Dust Bowl

What happens when cognitive surrender becomes a collective phenomenon?

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • AI may boost intellectual output while eroding independent thought.
  • Individual cognitive surrender may become a collective vulnerability.
  • An intellectual wasteland could be filled with brilliant answers.
Source: Image by WikiImages from Pixabay.

The Dust Bowl of the 1930s is one of America's great environmental catastrophes. We all remember the haunting images of dust and despair. But there's another story here that involves technology and the unintended consequences of progress.

Modern agriculture transformed the Great Plains, and farmers cultivated land with newfound efficiency. The high technology of the day—tractors and plows—helped turn the prairies into highly productive farmland. And in doing so, they disrupted the plant root structure that held the soil together. For a time, the land was productive. But then, the unintended consequences of both planning and purpose took root.

I've been thinking about this history lesson in the context of artificial intelligence, and I wonder if we're creating the conditions for something similar—an intellectual Dust Bowl.

The Productivity Paradox

I don't doubt that AI has provided us with amazing capabilities. We can generate "the answer" with little more than a simple prompt. And in this context, the Dust Bowl raises an interesting question about the relationship between this productivity and the technology that makes it happen. The key insight, buried until discovered, was that the land could produce tremendous quantities of wheat even as farming practices made that land precariously vulnerable.

Today, we're surrounded by evidence of AI's intellectual productivity—from the boardroom to the dining room. But I'm less certain (and more concerned) that we're paying attention to what's happening beneath those impressive results. Think (a word deliberately chosen) about the student who "produces" a quality essay without any real struggle, or the executive who "generates" a sophisticated market analysis without working through or even understanding the business nuances. The final product may be excellent, but something important may have been bypassed.

Thinking involves practices that aren't always efficient. In fact, it's often quite the contrary. The cognitive path from A to B is the terrain of discovery filled with contradictions and struggles, and these experiences allow us to learn and grow. AI offers a remarkably attractive and seductive alternative. But one that delivers a coherent answer before we've had much opportunity to traverse that landscape of discovery.

When Surrender Becomes Collective

I've written a good deal about cognitive surrender, and it's important to recognize the difference between surrender and delegation. Some of this delegation is useful and even liberating. But the Dust Bowl suggests that the more consequential impact of technology may emerge beyond the decisions you and I make individually.

Farmers across the Great Plains were often acting rationally. They adopted and adapted technology to support production and opportunity. But the accumulation of these decisions helped transform an entire economic and social landscape. It's interesting to note that the vulnerability was collective, even when individual choices appeared reasonable, if not a necessity.

Now consider millions of people making similar decisions about thinking—from a student taking the quick and simple path to the answer to a mathematician relying on AI to solve the unsolvable. None of these decisions represents a failure of judgment, but together they may begin changing what we expect from human intelligence.

And I think there's a deeper and important concern here. As AI-generated content becomes institutionalized, the independent and human reasoning behind that work can become less visible—maybe even less valued. What happens if our standards for originality shift toward evaluating the final product rather than the intellectual process that produced it? When that happens, we need to question if the very process of human innovation isn't just enhanced by technology, but compromised at a fundamental level.

The Abundance of Answers

What bothers me is that we might not recognize an intellectual Dust Bowl as it happens. We could continue producing amazing work with AI while becoming less proficient at independently generating it. Our objective measures of intellectual productivity might go up, while our capacity for independent judgment becomes more dependent on the technology supporting it. Sounds familiar, doesn't it?

Of course, AI can also deepen thought—the challenge of iterative intelligence versus cognitive surrender. The outcome depends in part on how we choose to use AI and how society rewards AI's computation. But I still wonder if the more revealing measure of progress could be our cognitive resilience—our ability to think and act when AI is wrong or when we need to reason without it.

The Dust Bowl eventually helped inspire new approaches to conservation, recognizing that agricultural productivity depended on protecting the soil itself. And I think there's a lesson here about preserving the intellectual practices that sustain (and protect) human thought, even as technology makes them easier to skip over.

We may be entering an era in which the abundance of intelligence actually tells us less and less about the health of human thinking. And that leaves us with a curious possibility of an intellectual wasteland filled with brilliant answers.

item.title: Is It Normal to Think About Leaving Your Partner?
item.description:
Relationships

Is It Normal to Think About Leaving Your Partner?

What thoughts of leaving can reveal about your relationship.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Thinking about leaving doesn’t automatically mean you no longer love your partner.
  • Address the problems behind your thoughts instead of bringing up separation during an argument.
  • Lasting improvement requires both partners to participate in repairing the relationship.

Naturally, most people commit to a relationship hoping it will last. What you may not realize is that even people who are genuinely happy with their partners occasionally imagine what life might be like if they were with someone else or even just single again.

Thoughts like these frequently pop up during periods of prolonged stress, emotional disconnect, or general conflict. People fantasize about living alone when they’re overwhelmed by household responsibilities or picture the relief of never again having to have an argument about an issue that keeps coming up over and over again.

Finding yourself thinking about leaving should be seen as a reason to take a fresh look at your relationship, but not an automatic signal to end it.

Does Thinking About Leaving Mean You No Longer Love Your Partner?

Love and relationship satisfaction may be related, but they’re ultimately two very different animals. Someone can stay consistently emotionally invested in their partner while also becoming increasingly frustrated with how the relationship functions on a practical level.

In a 2021 study involving 993 participants, researchers Brian Ogolsky and Laura Machia explored various reasons why people might consider either leaving their romantic relationships or staying in them. Love was cited as the most common reason for staying, while dissatisfaction was among the biggest reasons to leave. However, many of the subjects also expressed competing motivations.

It’s also worth noting that fantasies about leaving often reflect specific, potentially fixable problems. For example, a person dealing with deep resentment because they handle nearly every household responsibility themselves might fantasize about leaving despite also loving their partner. The issue is a specific problem—an unequal division of labor within the household—so the relationship might be able to recover if it improved. If the problem driving your desire to walk away weren’t an issue anymore, would you still want this relationship?

Do Happy People Fantasize About Leaving?

Even the healthiest, most loving relationships involve disagreements, conflicting needs, and periods when partners feel less connected. For that reason, occasionally thinking “what if” is normal and more compatible with general relationship satisfaction than people think.

Most fantasies of leaving fall into one of two categories:

Situational escape fantasies. These usually arise as stress responses to identifiable triggers, like difficult arguments or an unusually demanding week. Most have three important characteristics in common:

  • A specific circumstance or event triggers the thought.
  • Imagining separation provides relief from the immediate source of the stress.
  • The corresponding desire to leave dissipates once the problem is addressed or the emotional tension involved subsides.

For instance, it’s pretty normal for someone who’s just spent their whole weekend arguing with their partner to fantasize about enjoying freedom in an apartment of their own. However, a productive conversation and some quality time spent reconnecting might be all it takes to override the appeal of that fantasy.

Persistent escape fantasies. This type is more likely to develop over time due to unresolved long-term dissatisfaction. A person might start thinking about walking away from their relationship during ordinary, everyday moments that involve zero conflict. Some people may also feel relieved when their partner is out of town or even dread spending time together.

Patterns like these can be warning signs that relationship dissatisfaction extends beyond occasional or isolated disagreements. Does your desire to leave fade when nothing immediately stressful is going on, or does it stick around regardless of the circumstances?

Is It Temporary Frustration or a Sign You’re Ready to Leave?

Relationship researchers frequently use the term “dissolution consideration” to describe the process of ending an existing relationship. A 2009 study conducted by Laura VanderDrift and colleagues further found that dissolution consideration helped better explain the relationship between lower levels of commitment and actual behaviors associated with leaving.

Take a closer look and try to evaluate these three key indicators:

  • The persistence of the problem. Temporary problems and frustrations frequently improve with dedicated communication, compromises, or other changes in the circumstances of the relationship. Chronic dissatisfaction, on the other hand, recurs with little lasting improvement, despite repeated discussions and attempts to resolve it.
  • Your willingness to repair the relationship. How do you typically respond when opportunities for improvement present themselves? Are you genuinely motivated to communicate and rebuild connection with your partner, or do you feel emotionally disengaged from even the possibility of working things out?
  • Your expectations for the future. Can you realistically imagine a satisfying future with your partner? Make sure you’re accounting for their actual behavior and willingness to embrace compromise, as opposed to falling back on wishful thinking or relying solely on promises.

For a relationship to survive, both partners need to be willing (and able) to do things differently for the sake of the relationship.

Should You Tell Your Partner You’re Thinking About Leaving?

If you’ve been thinking about leaving lately, communicate with your partner about the underlying issue before putting separation on the table as a possible solution—and never just spontaneously tell a partner you’re thinking of leaving them in the middle of a heated argument. More often than not, that redirects the conversation toward defensiveness and away from the original problem.

Instead, address the actual dynamic or behavior fueling the dissatisfaction, so you both have something solid to unpack. For example, “When I try to talk about something that’s bothering me, and it turns into an argument, I feel discouraged about our ability to actually solve our problems together.”

(One important exception: In relationships that involve threats, coercive control, intimidation, or other forms of abuse, it can be dangerous to disclose existing or potential plans to leave. Seek confidential support and embrace safety planning in those situations.)

How Often Is Too Often to Think About Leaving?

There’s no clinical standard that definitively determines when your thoughts about leaving have reached a critical tipping point. Instead, assess your leaving fantasies according to frequency, emotional intensity, and consequences.

Many people also find it helpful to track these thoughts consistently for two weeks using the following method:

  • Trigger: What happened immediately before you started thinking about leaving?
  • Desired relief: What do you feel separating would finally let you change?
  • Persistence: Did the feelings go away after the situation improved?

Knowing the difference between recurring problems and temporary emotion-fueled reactions is the key to smart decisions you won’t regret later. (Individual or couples therapy might be a helpful consideration, as well.) The goal is to come to a well-considered conclusion based on the realities of the relationship you’re truly in.

item.title: October Is Conflict Resolution Month, Celebrated Worldwide
item.description:
Divorce

October Is Conflict Resolution Month, Celebrated Worldwide

For Conflict Resolution Month, a pioneer explains why skills beat blame.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Conflict is normal and okay on its own. High conflict is unhelpful and harmful.
  • Teaching skills for the future, rather than focusing on the past, is where change is possible.
  • The skills approach is much more positive than the shame and blame approach common in court.

This article is the first in a series that provides practical takeaways from three pioneers in family conflict resolution, who through their decades of experience have become internationally respected peacemakers and trainers of families and divorce professionals.

According to the Association for Conflict Resolution, a U.S. nonprofit organization, Conflict Resolution Day was conceived in 2005 to:

  • "Promote awareness of mediation, arbitration, conciliation and other creative, peaceful means of resolving conflict;
  • Promote the use of conflict resolution in schools, families, businesses, communities, governments and the legal system;
  • Recognize the significant contributions of (peaceful) conflict resolvers;
  • Obtain national synergy by having celebrations happen across the country and around the world on the same day."

October has become a time to promote and celebrate peaceful conflict resolution practices worldwide.

bphet / Pexels
Source: Celebrating peaceful conflict resolution practices worldwide

Gray divorce refers to divorce between couples aged 50 and older. To provide information about ways for gray divorce family members to resolve conflict, I spoke with Bill Eddy, LCSW, Esq., who is the pioneer of High Conflict Personality Theory, author of over 25 books, and the co-founder of the High Conflict Institute with Megan Hunter, MBA.

Carol Hughes: Looking back over your career, what experiences or realizations led you to believe there had to be a better way for families to resolve the conflicts of divorce?

Bill Eddy: I was trained in child and family counseling in 1980, when I got my master’s in social work degree. Included in our training was an introduction to personality disorders, which helped in several of my cases. I practiced part-time and full-time as a therapist over the next 12 years, including in a psychiatric hospital and an out-patient clinic. Many of my clients were involved in divorces and family court. I was already aware of mediation as a better out-of-court solution for most families, but if one parent wanted to go to court, that is where they ended up. I also recognized that many families involved in “high conflict” cases included one or two parents with personality disorders or traits. They really were not being well served in the adversarial process of court, so I wanted to make court and mediation fit their needs better. I believed that it would be better to calm the conflict and focus on teaching parents skills to be more successful, rather than to get stuck fighting.

CH: After decades of working with divorcing families, what is the one thing you most wish families understood about conflict during divorce?

BE: That the conflict can be managed by learning and practicing helpful skills yourself, rather than focusing on the other person. Even one person learning good communication and self-management skills can calm a conflict and help the children.

CH: At some point, you chose to extend your work beyond helping individual families to writing, teaching, and training other professionals. What inspired you to broaden your reach, and what did you hope would change as a result?

BE: I always like going to conferences and learning more about counseling, mediation, and law. I offered a workshop at one about dealing with personality disorders in mediation, and I expected 30 people, but 200 showed up! At that point in 2004, I realized there was a big need for all professionals to learn about personality disorders and skills for helping them resolve their disputes. That started me on a teaching and writing career, and I co-founded High Conflict Institute in 2008 to promote that.

CH: After all you have witnessed and learned over the course of your career, what gives you hope about the future of how families experience and resolve divorce conflict?

BE: I have seen many parents and families manage their conflicts better by learning a set of simple skills that I developed for the High Conflict Institute and which are being taught widely now: EAR [Empathy, Attention, and Respect] statements for verbally calming emotions; BIFF [Brief, Informative, Friendly, and Firm] emails and texts to end the written hostility; SLIC [Setting Limits and Imposing Consequences] solutions on high conflict behavior; SWYP [So, What's Your Proposal?] for making agreements in three steps; and New Ways for Families as an online class and counseling method for teaching all of these. The skills approach is much more positive than the shame and blame approach common in court.

CH: What is the biggest mistake well-meaning family members or professionals make when trying to calm a high-conflict divorce?

BE: Getting angry at people for not acting reasonably, when they don’t have the skills to do that yet. Trying to get people to have insight into their own behavior, focusing too much on the past, and opening up emotions makes things worse. Teaching skills to use in the future is where change is possible, but this takes a lot of repetition and practice, which family members and professionals should encourage. Getting difficult co-parents “on the other side” into structured programs to learn better skills is often necessary. That’s why we teach our New Ways for Families skills to both parents, so reasonable parents have some skills to use with the other parent, and high conflict parents have a structure to learn better skills in.

CH: What is the most important takeaway you want readers to know about conflict resolution?

BE: Conflict is normal and okay on its own. High conflict is unhelpful and can be harmful. Learning conflict resolution skills is something the whole family can do. That’s why we teach our New Ways for Families skills to parents and encourage them to teach their children as well. The “4 Big Skills” [flexible thinking, managed emotions, moderate behaviors, and checking yourself] that we teach can help them all for a lifetime.

In the next post, Canadian lawyer Jacinta Gallant shares how she uses curiosity, listening, and client preparation to lower conflict before families experiencing gray divorce begin creating solutions.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Why Your Brain Treats Your Bank Balance Like a Predator
item.description:
Stress

Why Your Brain Treats Your Bank Balance Like a Predator

Money avoidance brings relief, and that relief keeps the stress going.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Financial threats set off the same bodily stress response as physical danger.
  • Avoiding money tasks brings instant relief, and that relief teaches the brain to avoid them in the future.
  • The brain stays adaptable throughout life. Small, repeated finance-related actions build a new mental path.

In early spring in Northern Lapland, you can tell immediately where most cross-country skiers are heading. The popular tracks are packed smooth, often slippery, polished by thousands of pairs of skis. The more a track is used, the faster and easier it gets. Next to it, the unbroken snow leads into a cold, dark forest, tempting only the bravest of skiers.

Our brains work in a similar way. Each time we repeat a thought or behavior, the path gets a little easier to follow. Neuropsychologist Rick Hanson describes how even passing thoughts and feelings can leave a trace in the brain, much like rain cutting small channels into a hillside (Hanson, 2009). The brain saves energy by repeating what it already knows. Usually that is efficient, but it can also lock us into habits that hurt us.

The Relief Trap

My friend Irina grew up in a home where shopping trips with her mother meant warmth and closeness, but also secrecy, conflict, and guilt. As an adult, she feels uneasy whenever she must open her banking app. She pays her bills as fast as she can, usually on her phone while heading somewhere else. She glances at recent transactions and then quickly moves on to messaging a friend or picking a playlist.

Once the task is done, relief sets in. Her heart rate settles, her breathing slows, and her muscles relax. The danger has passed.

Each time Irina escapes the discomfort, her brain gets a small reward. Learning theory calls this negative reinforcement: a behavior that removes an unpleasant feeling becomes more likely to happen again. The avoidance track gets smoother. Meanwhile, the real consequences pile up. Irina often overdraws her account, rarely knows how much she has for unexpected costs, and manages her money by gut feeling. The brain gets better at spotting the financial “threat” and simultameously better at running from it.

A Funnel Built for Sabertooth Tigers

Why does managing our finances feel like a threat at all? The body’s stress response evolved for physical dangers. When our ancestors met a predator, their heart rate rose, adrenaline surged, and attention narrowed to the threat. It worked like a funnel, built to find the fastest way to survive. Running, hiding, or fighting were perfectly adequate solutions.

Today’s threats are different. Challenges like an overdue bill or rumors of layoffs are complex, faceless, and slow. Yet the body reacts in much the same way. The funnel that saved our ancestors now shuts out the information we need.

Daniel Kahneman (2011) described two modes of thinking. One is fast, intuitive, and emotional. The other is slow, deliberate, and effortful. Stress pushes us toward the fast mode, but financial problems usually need the slow one: comparing options, reading the fine print, planning ahead.

Research on poverty and cognition shows how much these matter. In a well-known series of studies, Mani and colleagues (2013) found that simply asking lower-income participants to think about a difficult financial scenario lowered their performance on cognitive tests. The drop was about as large as the effect of losing a full night’s sleep. Sugarcane farmers in India also did better on the same tests after harvest, when money was plentiful, than before harvest, when it was tight. Their conclusion was that financial worry uses up mental bandwidth. A mind occupied by money worries is not well-equipped to solve money problems.

The Worry Trap

The opposite of avoidance is worrying, and it is easy to mistake for responsibility; if you lie awake running numbers, you believe, then you must be taking your finances seriously.

But worrying is like spinning your wheels in heavy snow: It feels like movement but gets you nowhere. Research on worry has found that negative, repetitive thinking impairs how we process information and make decisions (Metzger et al., 1990). Worry also fools us into feeling we have done something when nothing has changed. Action is different: even imperfect steps teach us something while worry keeps us circling the same spot.

Financial stress is not just unpleasant; it adds up. Studies of financially distressed consumers link money strain with poorer self-reported health (O’Neill et al., 2005). A life-course study found that people who had faced financial hardship repeatedly over many years had worse health in older age, even after accounting for their current finances (Kahn & Pearlin, 2006). Financial stress also spills into relationships and is linked to more conflict and poorer relationship outcomes (Hubler et al., 2016).

The encouraging side is that the link runs in both directions. In a randomized controlled trial with low-income single mothers, a program of financial education and coaching was associated with improvements in health (White et al., 2022). When people feel more financially secure, they tend to rest more, look after themselves better, and cope better with everyday setbacks.

Carving a New Trail

It was long believed that the adult brain was essentially a fixed entity, but now we know better. The brain keeps adapting to experience throughout life, although change in deeper emotional systems can be slow and takes repetition (Merzenich, 2013). The practical implication is that you do not need to feel ready before you start. Readiness comes from practice.

Some ways to start skiing off the familiar track:

  • Make contact brief and regular. Rather than avoiding your finances until the last moment, try a short, scheduled look each week. This can show your nervous system that looking is okay.
  • Turn worry into one step. When the wheels start spinning, ask, “What is one thing I can actually do?” Then do it, even if it is small.
  • Build a small buffer. Even a modest cushion in your account can calm the stress response. It leaves room for the slow, deliberate thinking that good financial decisions require.
  • Get support. Financial counselors, coaches, and trusted friends can help lighten the load, and the pressure on your mental bandwidth.

The first few runs through fresh snow are slow and tiring. But every trip makes the new trail a little easier, until one day it's become the path you take without thinking.

item.title: Why Is It So Hard To Know What I Need?
item.description:
Defense Mechanisms

Why Is It So Hard To Know What I Need?

The needs we can't meet alone are often the ones we never notice.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Deeper needs like love and belonging require other people, which makes them feel risky and out of our control.
  • A protective part may steer attention away before a need surfaces with ease.
  • Parts work helps: It’s easier to accept that part of us has a need than that the whole of us does.

If you’re anything like me, you read the title of a post like that and instantly go — that’s not me. I know what I need. When I’m hungry, I go for a snack. I can assess whether I want something salty or sweet, see if we have anything in the fridge that satisfies my craving, and if not, order something on an app that will be at my door in 30 minutes or less. Check. Gold star! I win at meeting my needs.

But that’s not the kind of need that I want to bring into the mix today. In Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, those are pretty close to the bottom of the pyramid. Physiological needs, safety, and security are important, but what about something deeper, like love or belonging? I want you to think back to a moment when you felt alone. Maybe you read the news and felt a sense of dread. Maybe you had a tough conversation with a family member. Maybe things just felt really heavy, and you couldn’t find hope to hold on to. What did you need in that moment?

Oh, I’ll wait.

Why is needing other people so hard?

I say this with love and compassion, but for many of us who consider ourselves competent, strong, and successful, we have no idea how to be with those deeper needs. And I think one reason why is quite simple: Those needs require other people. And other people introduce an element of chance, of chaos, of lack of control. My snack dilemma is completely within my control. I don’t need anyone else (except maybe the app-based delivery driver) to fulfill my craving for chips and salsa. But a moment when I’m having trouble finding something to be hopeful for? What if the friend I reach out to for comfort doesn't have time for me? What if my partner is afraid of my hopelessness and views me as broken? Needing something from someone else is risky. It asks us to be vulnerable. And for many of us, that just isn’t tolerable.

The worst part of this is I don’t even give myself the chance to have this inner conversation. It’s not like I look at what I need and make a conscious choice that it isn’t worth the risk. Something inside me senses the danger and shuts the whole thing down before the need ever surfaces. And so I go right on believing that I am totally self-sufficient and addressing my needs like a mental health champ.

So, how do we begin to address an unknown unknown? If we’re so good at turning away from these needs before they even arrive in our awareness, how can we ever get good at meeting them?

How do you notice a need you can’t see?

Remember when I asked you to picture a time you felt alone and to figure out what you needed then? I’m curious — did you actually land on something, or did you suddenly find yourself thinking about what you’re making for dinner, or your growing to-do list, or the path of that butterfly that just flew by your window? I’m willing to bet that you didn’t do it consciously. Rather, something inside you started to stir, and your attention left the building.

I often find this focus shift to feel quite light and easy — almost as if that part of me is saying, “pay no attention to the man behind the curtain,” everything is fine, carry on as you were. Sometimes in my own therapy, when I get close to something painful, it quite literally feels like I bounce off of it, like there's a force field around it. I’m tapping into some sadness and then, boop, I wonder if that new Netflix show has good reviews. And while I might not be able to delve into the need that is there, I am becoming more aware of the bounce.

What if part of you doesn’t want to know?

Once I recognize the bounce, I find it helpful to think about our inner worlds as made up of parts. The way I explain it to clients is like this: You know when you’re staring at a menu, and some part of you wants the pasta but another part of you wants the chicken? It’s just like that, except one part of you has a need and the other is trying to protect you from being hurt. In Ego State Therapy (one approach for working with parts), we spend time getting to know each part. And parts work isn’t a diagnosis; it's just a way of describing what many of us already feel. Sometimes, I name the parts. Maybe one part is Frodo Baggins carrying the heavy weight of the ring and the other part is Gandalf trying to protect the hobbit from harm. Many of us can accept that a part of us has a need. It’s much easier than accepting that the whole of us does.

I find it helpful to acknowledge to Gandalf that you know he’s just trying to protect you and Frodo. Thank him for all his support. But maybe ask if you can spend some time talking to Frodo. Get to know him. See if he has any dreams for you, any yearnings, or any needs.

The harder I try to force these deeper needs to surface, the more activated my force field becomes. But when I slow down, notice what’s actually going on, and start engaging the parts of myself in conversation, things start to shift. Take a second and remember that moment you felt alone. Notice the protective part that rushes in to tell you everything is fine. Thank him for trying to keep you safe. Really mean it. Then turn to your inner ringbearer, carrying the weight of the world on his shoulders, and ask him what he needs. And listen.
